title: Krishna Steals the Gopis' Clothes
story:
For a full month the young women of Vrindavan had kept their vow. Through the coldest days of early winter they rose before dawn, walked down to the Yamuna together, and bathed in water that took the breath away. Each morning they worshipped the goddess with sandal paste, garlands, incense, and small lamps of ghee, and each morning the prayer was the same: that Krishna, the dark and lovely son of Nanda and the cowherd boy of their own village, might one day be their own. It was a shy, impossible prayer, the kind young hearts make and tell no one but the river.

These were the girls who had stood shivering in the river every dawn, asking a goddess to grant them this very boy. They had pictured him a hundred ways — on the path at dusk, at the festival, across the fields. None of them had pictured him like this: perched high in a tree with their own clothes heaped beside him, grinning down as if the whole long winter had been leading to this one joke.

That morning, as on every other, they laid their clothes on the riverbank and stepped into the water. But this time Krishna had come down to the river after them, and he understood at once what their long discipline had really been for; nothing of their hearts was hidden from him. Quietly he gathered the garments from the bank, and before any of them could turn, he had climbed a kadamba tree and settled among its branches, the bundle of clothes laid beside him like a prize. The tree stood close to the water, its leaves dark and heavy in the grey morning light.

From the branches he laughed and called down to them. "Come," he said, "one by one, and take back what is yours."

The girls stood waist-deep in the cold river and looked up at him. They did not grow angry, and they did not sink away and hide. They remembered that he had never once spoken an untruth to them, and that there was no cruelty in this jest, and so they did not reproach him. One by one their heads lifted, and they stole glances at one another across the water, unsure whether to laugh or to plead. All their dawn baths, all their whispered prayers, had been aimed at him; and here he was, suddenly, within arm's reach, asking them to set down the last of their shyness and stand before him as they were. They only looked up — and they were flooded with love, the way a lamp flares when a hand is cupped too near the flame.

Krishna gave no sign of climbing down. He knew them, and he knew the prayer that had sent them into the water day after day; the whole jest turned on that knowing. The clothes stayed high in the tree, and the girls stayed in the river, and between them hung a question neither side moved to answer.

The morning was very still. The current slid past, dark and cold, the leaves of the kadamba barely stirred, and the sound of his laughter still hung in the air above the water. The water lapped against them, cold as it had been all month, but none of them moved to cover themselves or to go; they only stood, and looked up, and loved him.
reflection: The jest is not mockery. Krishna takes the one thing the girls would be ashamed to be seen without, and by doing so he strips away the shyness that stood between them and the one they had been praying for. The verse marks no anger in them — only love — because they trust that his mischief has no cruelty in it.
next_story_tease: But the clothes stayed high in the tree, and the girls still shivered in the river, waiting to see what he would ask of them.
hero_scene: Krishna sitting high in a kadamba tree on the Yamuna's bank, a bundle of the gopis' garments beside him, laughing down at the young women who stand waist-deep in the cold river looking up at him.
